w: Funded by private donations and unveiled in 1935, this 42-metre granite-and-copper column honours soldiers of the 1918-1920 War of Independence, Liberty lifting three gilded stars at its top. Soviet occupiers marked it for demolition after 1940 - the story goes sculptor Vera Mukhina helped save it instead.
s: 42 metres of granite the Soviets meant to tear down
_facts: Unveiled in 1935, financed by private donations, honours soldiers of the 1918-1920 Latvian War of Independence
42-metre monument of granite, travertine and copper; Liberty figure lifts three gilded stars atop a 19-metre travertine column
Thirteen sculpted groups depict Latvian culture and history
After the 1940 Soviet occupation it was considered for demolition but survived, sometimes credited to Soviet sculptor Vera Mukhina

w: Founded on the Daugava in 1330, this fortress has been rebuilt by nearly every power that held Riga - overhauled in 1497-1515, expanded by the conquering Swedes in 1641, remodelled through the 17th-19th centuries. Declared the government's seat in 1938, it is now the President's residence and home to several museums.
s: A 1330 fortress rebuilt by every power that took Riga
_facts: Founded in 1330 on the banks of the River Daugava
Rebuilt 1497-1515; Swedes seized it and added annexes in 1641; further reconstruction through the 17th-19th centuries
Declared the Latvian government's residence in 1938
Today the official residence of the President of Latvia and home to several museums

w: Billed as Europe's largest market, its five soaring pavilions rose in 1924-1930 by recycling German Zeppelin hangars into Neoclassical and Art Deco halls. Over 3,000 stalls trade across 72,300 square metres, and the complex has shared UNESCO World Heritage status with Old Riga since 1998.
s: Zeppelin hangars turned into Europe's biggest market
_facts: Billed as Europe's largest market and bazaar; planned from 1922, built 1924-1930
Five pavilions built by reusing old German Zeppelin hangars, in Neoclassicism and Art Deco styles
72,300 square metres wide with more than 3,000 trade stands
Included on the UNESCO World Heritage list together with Old Riga since 1998

w: Built in Neo-Byzantine style in 1876-1883 with the Tsar's blessing, this became the Baltic provinces' largest Orthodox cathedral, its icons said to include work by painter Vasili Vereshchagin. Soviet authorities closed it in the 1960s and installed a planetarium inside; it has served as a cathedral again since 1991.
s: A cathedral the Soviets turned into a planetarium
_facts: Built 1876-1883 in Neo-Byzantine style by Nikolai Chagin and Robert Pflug, with the blessing of Tsar Alexander II
Largest Orthodox cathedral in the Baltic provinces; icons include work attributed to Vasili Vereshchagin
German occupiers converted it to a Lutheran church in WWI; it returned to Orthodox use in 1921
Soviet authorities closed it in the early 1960s and converted it into a planetarium; restored as a cathedral since 1991, with the bell tower and dome gilded in 2010
